Abstract

Maintaining coherent agentic work becomes an architectural challenge as information, participants, commitments, execution components, and operating conditions change. This paper proposes Agentic AI 2.0, a system-level architectural framework that integrates established concepts to organize ongoing goal-directed work in foundation-model-based systems. Six constitutive properties characterize this organization: Maintained Process State, Collective Coordination, Shared Operational Knowledge, Governed and Grounded Action, Computational Continuity, and Feedback-Driven Adaptation. The framework connects these properties to role-bearing agents, shared operational objects, interface contracts, and interacting execution, coordination, and adaptation loops. A composition guard specifies how local acceptance decisions connect across operational boundaries, while a criterion-level codebook supports configuration-specific assessment from explicit evidence. We examine the framework through a constructed production-order trace, disruption and handoff branches, counterexamples, and static source profiles of three application configurations and one infrastructure boundary case. The analyses distinguish local feasibility from joint commitments, effect reconciliation from execution-right control, and retained skill versions from governed activation and reuse. They also separate scoped negative evidence from unresolved evidence when diagnosing architectural relationships. Candidate evaluation and later reuse remain conditional in the worked example. Prospective profiles for enterprise productivity, adaptive manufacturing, and distributed mobility identify domain-specific evidence needs and evaluation priorities. The contribution is a traceable basis for architectural analysis, comparison, and design. Independent assessor studies, comparative diagnosis, and controlled and longitudinal implementation studies are needed to establish its practical value and the relationship between architectural choices, operational outcomes, and cost.

Keywords: Agentic AI; foundation models; multi-agent systems; reference architecture; architectural analysis; computational continuity; AI governance

1. Introduction

Foundation models support agents that interpret goals, reason over intermediate steps, use tools, and interact with external environments. ReAct connects reasoning and action through environmental observations [1], while Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA) organizes memory, actions, and decision processes [2]. Computer-use benchmarks extend this setting to desktop applications and tasks combining graphical interaction with command-line and code execution [3, 4]. Maintaining work across these interactions introduces architectural questions about state, responsibility, and the evidence on which subsequent decisions depend.

1.1. From Task Execution to Ongoing Work

Consider a production order involving planning, procurement, machine operation, and quality control. A machine failure may invalidate an accepted allocation. An executor may become unavailable after issuing an action whose external effect remains uncertain. Another executor must then determine which obligations remain and whether dependent work can resume. Experience from the disruption may inform a later order, subject to the conditions under which that experience applies.

We use ongoing autonomous work for goal-directed work that can span pauses, authorized human decisions, changes in responsible actors, and recovery from disruption. Its organization must preserve the information and responsibilities needed for subsequent decisions. Role-based workflows, retained memory, and reusable skills provide relevant mechanisms [2, 5, 6]. Their contribution depends on how they connect to the same undertaking across interactions and execution episodes.

1.2. Architectural Concern and Contributions

The architectural concern is the connection between capability outputs and their operational consequences. Observations require acceptance before they change maintained state; proposed plans require authority and compatible commitments before they allocate work. Execution requests require environmental evidence to establish their outcomes. Component changes require reconciliation and authority to continue, while reusable changes require evaluation and context-specific adoption.

Collaborative planning and normative multi-agent systems provide foundations for commitments, roles, permissions, and obligations [7, 8, 9]. Distributed recovery addresses the relationship between restored computation and prior external effects [10]. We bring these concerns together around the records and acceptance responsibilities of ongoing foundation-model-based work.

This paper proposes Agentic AI 2.0, a system-level architectural framework connecting accepted state, commitments, authority, outcome evidence, continuation, and versioned change. The designation identifies an architectural orientation rather than a chronological generation or maturity level. Its unit of analysis is a declared configuration and operational scope, including the actors, execution components, interfaces, authority arrangements, and changes relevant to the assessed work.

The paper makes three contributions:

  1. Architectural characterization and profiling. Six constitutive properties define the proposed family. A configuration-specific codebook distinguishes established relationships, scoped negative witnesses, and unresolved evidence, with explicit rules for deriving a property-level profile.

  2. Reference architecture. Role-bearing agents, shared operational objects, interface contracts, and execution, coordination, and adaptation loops specify how the relevant responsibilities connect. Acceptance conditions identify when information, proposals, actions, and changes acquire an operational status.

  3. Architectural analysis. Comparison with close predecessors, a constructed production-order trace, witness requirements, changed-condition checks, counterexamples, and implementation-source profiles make selected relationships inspectable. Diagnostic findings identify affected decisions, supporting evidence, and follow-up checks; application profiles examine their implications in three domains.

The analysis supports examination of the proposed distinctions within its declared cases and evidence. Independent profiling reliability, comparative diagnostic value, and effects on operational performance form the evaluation agenda in Section 7.

Sections 2 and 3 establish the positioning, definitions, and profiling rules. Sections 4–5 develop the mechanisms and architecture. Sections 6–8 present the analysis, application profiles, discussion, and conclusions.

2. Architectural Foundations and Positioning

The framework draws on research in agent organization, maintained work state, conditional progression, recovery, and adaptation. This targeted comparison identifies the abstractions inherited by the synthesis and the relationships examined through its operational perspective.

2.1. Architectural Foundations for Ongoing Work

Cognitive architectures organize memory, reasoning, and learning within an agent. Soar, for example, combines working memory and problem-space reasoning with chunking [11]. Distributed cognition extends the analytical boundary to information use across people, artifacts, and external representations [12]. These perspectives inform the distinction between an individual agent’s retained information and knowledge used across operational responsibilities.

Organizational and collaborative approaches provide direct precedents for responsibility allocation and commitments. Gaia models roles, permissions, interactions, and organizational rules [13]; SharedPlans formalizes partial plans, allocated actions, and commitments to joint activity [7]. STEAM connects joint intentions to communication, responsibility monitoring, and team reorganization [8]. Electronic institutions and normative multi-agent systems address protocols, obligations, permissions, and enforcement [9, 14].

Work-centered models connect maintained information to progression conditions. Guard-Stage-Milestone (GSM) couples business-entity information with guards, stages, and milestones, while adaptive case management examines changes to artifact-centric behavior and preservation conditions [15, 16]. Autonomic computing contributes component interfaces and feedback-based management: White et al. [17] describe interacting autonomic components and prototype studies, and IBM’s blueprint organizes monitor, analyze, plan, and execute functions around shared knowledge [18].

Recovery adds requirements concerning external effects. Rollback-recovery protocols account for communication dependencies and outputs beyond the recovering computation [10]. Chubby’s recipient-checked sequencers illustrate control of stale execution rights at the protected interface [19]. Workflow patterns, process mining, and continual learning contribute control-flow structures, analysis of execution records, and retention and transfer under change, respectively [20, 21, 22].

Table 1 identifies the closest architectural precedents and the connections developed in this paper.

The comparison identifies conceptual antecedents. Property-level support requires assessment of a selected configuration under Section 3.3. Section 2.4 considers a composition of these predecessors as an analytical comparator.

2.2. Contemporary Agentic Mechanisms and Evidence

Contemporary agents connect perception, reasoning, action, and learning through several mechanisms. ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions and observations, while Language Agent Tree Search combines search, value estimates, reflection, and external feedback [1, 23]. CoALA provides a memory-and-action account of the individual language agent [2]. AutoGen supports programmable conversations among models, tools, and humans [24]. CAMEL studies role-playing cooperation [25], while MetaGPT organizes software development through role-specific procedures and intermediate artifacts [5].

Computer-use benchmarks connect agent behavior to environmental outcomes. OSWorld includes desktop and web tasks with execution-based evaluation [3]. WeaveBench examines hybrid graphical user interface (GUI)–command-line interface (CLI)/code workflows and trajectory-aware evaluation [4]. Other benchmarks address policy-following reliability and prompt-injection robustness [26, 27]; evaluation methodology also considers repeated-trial reliability and the cost of obtaining a result [28].

Reflexion retains verbal reflections [29], while Voyager accumulates executable skills from environmental feedback [6]. Agent Workflow Memory derives reusable workflows [30], and A-Mem revises a linked memory network [31]. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) uses multi-step interaction data for policy updates [32, 33]. These mechanisms provide different objects of adaptation, with distinct conditions for their subsequent operational use.

Recent continuity preprints examine checkpoint/resume contracts [34], security-relevant rollback dependencies [35], transactional tool progress [36], durable workflow recovery [37], and event-sourced handoff across coding agents [38]. Related work addresses persistent memory, governance, and longer-horizon reliability [39, 40]. Together, these studies motivate assessment of how restored state, external effects, outstanding commitments, and authority connect within a supported continuation path.

Empirical studies also motivate attention to process behavior. Cemri et al. [41] derive MAST from 150 traces and release over 1,600 annotated traces across seven frameworks, identifying 14 failure modes in system design, inter-agent misalignment, and task verification. Their reported failure rates apply to the evaluated framework–benchmark configurations. Rabanser et al. [42] examine 15 models on GAIA and τ\tau-bench and report limited reliability gains relative to task-performance improvements. These findings motivate architectural questions about coordination and verification; the validity of the proposed profiling procedure remains a separate evaluation question.

2.3. Agentic Operating Systems and Shared Infrastructure

We use Agentic Operating System (Agentic OS) for infrastructure supplying shared services to agents. AIOS provides agent-oriented kernel services, while Borg supplies a precedent for cluster resource management [43, 44]. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) specifies tool discovery and invocation, and Agent2Agent (A2A) specifies agent discovery and task-oriented interaction [45, 46]. Other proposals address identifiers, certification, rollback, and broader operating infrastructure [47, 48].

These services can support the reference architecture through scheduling, storage, access control, and execution management. Their operational significance depends on the application responsibilities and acceptance conditions they implement. Resource capacity and technical permissions must therefore be related to the commitments and authority of the assessed work.

2.4. Positioning and Scope of the Architectural Synthesis

The synthesis organizes inherited abstractions around the same ongoing foundation-model-based work. Shared operational objects connect its state, commitments, authority, actions, and changes; interface contracts identify the conditions for changing their operational status. develop this reference organization.

A composition of artifact lifecycles, organizational agent models, recovery and execution-right controls, and policy-governed adaptation provides a substantive analytical comparator. Such a composition could realize the proposed responsibilities. The question examined here is how these responsibilities connect: an Action Record refers to the work, plan version, executor, authority, and outcome evidence; handoff accounts for that action and the remaining commitments; and a reusable change identifies its accepted version and applicable work. Execution-right control, responsibility transfer, and change applicability each require evidence within this connected account.

The comparison follows each source’s unit of analysis and evidence scope. Publication status is recorded separately from evidence type: formal results concern their models and assumptions, implementations their identified configurations, evaluations their tested conditions, and technical specifications their interface scope. Author-reported findings and independent validation remain distinguishable. Unreported relationships are evidence gaps.

Section 3.2 explains the retrospective construction of the six properties from these antecedents. The worked example and configuration profiles examine selected consequences of the proposed organization. Relative expressive power and comparative diagnostic accuracy require the independent comparisons outlined in Section 7.

3. Framework and Architectural Profiling

The framework characterizes how a bounded configuration organizes ongoing work. Its application requires explicit definitions of the undertaking, participating actors, supported changes, and evidence used for assessment.

3.1. Definition and Unit of Analysis

Definition 1. Agentic AI 2.0

Agentic AI 2.0 denotes a system-level architectural organization in which ongoing goal-directed work is maintained through explicit process state, coordinated across participating agent roles, supported by shared operational knowledge, and advanced through governed and grounded action. The organization supports continuation across specified changes in execution components and uses feedback to guide controlled adaptation and the accumulation of reusable experience.

A model supplies cognitive capabilities for interpretation, reasoning, planning, or action selection. A harness connects these capabilities to context, memory, tools, execution control, validation, guardrails, and tracing as required by the operational scope. A runtime provides their software execution environment. These functions may share a package or be distributed across services.

A role specifies an expected contribution, responsibilities, and a decision or action scope. An operational actor is an identifiable bearer of those responsibilities. An agent is a software operational actor with an assigned role; humans may also hold operational responsibilities and authority. An actor boundary requires a separately attributable assignment, a defined decision or action scope, and traceable consequences of its contributions, such as changes to accepted state, commitments, actions, or another actor’s evidence. A planner, critic, dispatcher, or store operating within another actor’s assignment remains an internal or supporting component.

These mappings are many-to-many: an actor may perform several roles and use multiple models or services, while several actors may share a model and runtime. Actors may contribute sequentially when their separate assignments and interdependencies remain identifiable. Collective Coordination requires distinct agent actors; human participation is assessed through the information, authority, or decisions it contributes. The configuration may operate within an organization or another environment.

A process denotes organized goal-directed work, including its state, dependencies, commitments, and completion conditions, rather than an operating-system process. A work episode is a bounded undertaking that may span several runtime execution episodes. Process identity associates those episodes with a stable reference, or an explicit mapping between references, accepted terms, and authorized revision history. An amendment remains within the same undertaking when the declared identity rule recognizes it and records its consequences for existing obligations. A different undertaking is recorded as a successor, with its predecessor relationship and the disposition of inherited or outstanding obligations.

Execution lineage records derivation among runs, checkpoints, branches, or configurations. Valid continuation establishes whether the identified process may proceed under its state, commitments, evidence, compatibility conditions, responsibility, and authority. Identity and lineage support traceability; admissibility of the next transition requires these continuation conditions.

An agent lifetime covers the actor’s existence and operational history under the applicable identity and versioning rules. A process lifetime runs from establishment to completion or authorized termination, including pauses and changes in participation. One process may span several agent lifetimes, and an agent may contribute to several work episodes.

The unit of analysis is a specific system configuration within a declared operational scope, with identified versions and specified changes under consideration. The scope covers the workload, actors and roles, models, harnesses, runtimes, shared services, environment interfaces, authority arrangements, and environmental assumptions relevant to the work. Here, ongoing work includes suspension, handoff, and authorized termination. Section 3.3 specifies the evidence needed to characterize this unit.

3.2. Constitutive Architectural Properties

The six properties specify the requirements adopted for this architectural family. Their construction is a retrospective analytical reconstruction of the targeted comparison in Section 2.4. The source abstractions are interpreted as relations among work, information, responsible actors, and the conditions governing operational use or change. A concept is retained at the property level when it identifies a work-level responsibility with a distinguishable assessment question; retrieval, tool invocation, checkpointing, and model updating are mechanisms that can support those responsibilities.

The properties are interdependent, and their minimality and exhaustiveness remain open to evaluation. Table 2 summarizes their assessment questions. Appendix A gives the constituent criteria, grouping alternatives, and boundary cases.

3.2.1. Maintained Process State

The system maintains an identifiable account of accepted goals and completion conditions, progress, dependencies, unfinished obligations, and relevant environmental conditions across execution episodes. State-acceptance and version rules distinguish received information from the current operational account. Uncertainty and unresolved conditions remain visible where they affect subsequent decisions. This property concerns the accepted condition of the undertaking and its use in determining what remains to be done.

3.2.2. Collective Coordination

Distinct agent actors in interdependent roles make attributable contributions that affect planning, allocation, or revision of the same work. Coordination allocates responsibilities, manages dependencies and resource conflicts, and establishes or revises commitments. A commitment records an accepted undertaking attributed to a responsible actor through its current role assignment, with conditions governing its application or revision. Assessment examines how conflicting proposals and changed conditions lead to authorized dispositions of affected plans and commitments.

3.2.3. Shared Operational Knowledge

Information is accumulated, retrieved, and made usable across distinct operational actors under contextual, access, and validity conditions. Consumers must be able to distinguish observations, assumptions, knowledge claims, decisions, and outcomes, together with relevant provenance, temporal context, and versions. Conflict and supersession rules preserve these distinctions during use. Linked stores and role-specific views may provide this support. Maintained Process State identifies the accepted situation of an undertaking; Shared Operational Knowledge concerns information used across responsibilities to interpret and act within it.

3.2.4. Governed and Grounded Action

Actions proceed under applicable authority, preconditions, and constraints, through interfaces connected to the declared environment. Outcome acceptance uses evidence attributable to the requested operation. Authority to act, dispatch admission, and confirmation of an effect are separate judgments attached to the same action. Failure and uncertainty remain explicit when subsequent decisions concern waiting, investigation, retry, escalation, or dependent execution.

3.2.5. Computational Continuity

The configuration supports valid continuation of identified work across specified interruptions or changes to agents, models, harnesses, runtimes, or shared infrastructure. Continuation accounts for accepted terms, unfinished commitments, prior effects, and the receiving configuration’s compatibility. Responsibility and authority are retained, transferred, or re-established, with overlapping execution rights resolved. The claim is bounded by the named changes and their reconciliation, compatibility, and authority conditions.

3.2.6. Feedback-Driven Adaptation

Feedback informs candidate changes or retained experience intended for later work. Candidates undergo evaluation against declared acceptance conditions; activation identifies the accepted version, applicability, and affected work and dependencies. Reuse links the retained version and application context to outcome feedback. Changes may concern knowledge, skills, workflows, planning policies, or model parameters. Evaluation may support adoption, revision, rejection, or withdrawal. Current-work plan repair and cross-work reuse remain distinct, and performance benefits require evidence beyond the existence of this pathway.

Table 2. Architectural properties and assessment questions.
Property Assessment question Evidence to examine
P1 Maintained Process State What is the accepted condition of the undertaking across execution episodes? Work references, accepted terms, state use, uncertainty, update decisions, and versions.
P2 Collective Coordination How do interdependent agent contributions establish and revise shared commitments? Actor assignments, allocations, dependencies, conflict resolution, and commitment dispositions.
P3 Shared Operational Knowledge What information can another responsible actor use, and under which conditions? Contributors and consumers, operational use, provenance, status, validity, and access rules.
P4 Governed and Grounded Action What authorizes the action, admits its execution, and establishes its outcome? Authority, preconditions, interfaces, request-linked evidence, and outcome dispositions.
P5 Computational Continuity Under what conditions may identified work continue across a specified change? Reconciliation, compatibility, outstanding obligations, responsibility, authority, and execution-right control.
P6 Feedback-Driven Adaptation How does feedback become evaluated change and governed reuse in later work? Candidate versions, evaluation, acceptance, activation, dependencies, reuse context, and outcome feedback.

The questions summarize the proposed architectural requirements. Coding follows the complete criteria in Tables A1 and A2; examples admit equivalent mechanisms. Support is scoped to the claim basis in Section 3.3.

Figure 1 presents structural and temporal views of these relationships. The panels describe complementary aspects of the work; their conceptual groupings permit different actor counts, topologies, and deployment arrangements.

3.3. Architectural Profiles and Transitional Systems

Assessment first declares the workload and work-episode boundaries, configuration versions and enabled components, actor assignments, interfaces and external services, authority and trust assumptions, supported changes, excluded conditions, and available evidence. External services contribute when their applicable contracts and evidence are identified; dependencies remain part of the assessment even when supplied outside the deployment boundary. Computational Continuity requires at least one named interruption or change and its continuation conditions.

Judgments follow operational relationships. Repackaging equivalent responsibilities, decision scopes, and dependencies leaves a profile unchanged when its evidence is equivalent. Changes in the configuration, assessment boundary, available evidence, or codebook are recorded separately so that reassessment can identify what changed.

Codebook v1.0 comprises 21 criteria in Appendix A: three each for P1–P3 and four each for P4–P6. Each record retains the criterion identifier, scope, applicable conditions, source and version, evidence, counterevidence, unresolved questions, code, and rationale. The claim basis is recorded independently of the code:

  • D: specification—an explicitly described responsibility or procedure;

  • I: implementation—its realization in an identified configuration;

  • O: observed behavior—particular executions under stated conditions;

  • V: evaluated behavior—behavior assessed under an identified protocol, cases, and reported outcomes.

Each basis bounds the conclusion it supports. Direct source inspection, author-reported implementation, and execution by the assessor retain their respective provenance. Separate bases may yield separate profiles for the same configuration.

Each criterion receives one code:

  1. Established (E): admissible evidence establishes the complete criterion at the declared basis and scope. Evidence for only some constituent obligations is retained as a narrower finding.

  2. Not satisfied (N): admissible evidence establishes an excluded, omitted, or violated required relationship within scope. The record identifies the failed obligation and a configuration-matched negative witness; equivalent mechanisms are assessed by the relationship they realize.

  3. Unknown (U): evidence establishes neither E nor N. This includes missing information, unexamined conditions, uncertain source applicability, or unresolved material source conflicts.

Admissible evidence addresses the same criterion, configuration, version, conditions, and claim basis. A confirmed in-scope counterexample yields N even when other included cases have positive evidence. Unresolved disagreement about source applicability or the validity of a counterexample yields U. A rejection or suspended handoff can establish support when that disposition is required by the criterion.

All criteria are required for complete characterization. Applicability qualifies condition-dependent obligations within a criterion: a conflict-handling branch may be unnecessary when its trigger is demonstrably excluded, while the remaining coordination requirements still apply. Positive relationships, including cross-actor use and continuation across a named change, require affirmative evidence; an empty declared domain cannot establish them. Unknown applicability remains an evidence gap.

For property ii, let RiR_i be its nonempty set of codebook criteria, and let eie_i, nin_i, and uiu_i count its E, N, and U codes, respectively, with mi=|Ri|=ei+ni+uim_i = |R_i| = e_i+n_i+u_i. The property label is

Li={NS,ni>0,S,ei=mi,PS,ni=0,ei>0,ui>0,II,ui=mi.L_i = \begin{cases} \mathrm{NS}, & n_i > 0,\\ \mathrm{S}, & e_i = m_i,\\ \mathrm{PS}, & n_i = 0,\ e_i > 0,\ u_i > 0,\\ \mathrm{II}, & u_i = m_i. \end{cases}(1)

The cases are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. S denotes Supported within scope; NS, Not satisfied within scope; PS, Partially supported by available evidence; and II, Insufficient information. This is a logical aggregation of evidence, rather than a coverage percentage or maturity score.

NS records at least one unmet requirement and may coexist with established mechanisms. PS records partial knowledge with at least one E and no N. For example, a handoff that retains state but demonstrably drops an outstanding commitment can establish P5.1 and violate P5.2, yielding NS. If commitment handling is unreported, P5.2 remains U and the property is PS provided no criterion receives N. All four continuity criteria must receive E for S.

One source may support several criteria when each use has its own rationale. A supported profile must draw on compatible configurations, versions, workloads, and claim bases. For relationships between acceptance boundaries, evidence must connect the exchanged claim, dependency and version bindings, and receiving-use conditions, as specified in Section 4.4.1. A coding judgment describes that evidence; operational authorization remains a separate decision. Appendix D records the criterion vectors and source locators used in Section 6.4.

A complete Agentic AI 2.0 characterization requires S for all six properties at a compatible configuration, scope, codebook version, and claim basis. NS identifies an unmet requirement; PS and II identify incomplete support. Transitional systems describes configurations with established relationships alongside unresolved or unmet requirements. Where used, Agentic AI 1.0 also denotes a stated architectural profile. These terms specify neither a development sequence nor task suitability; performance and reliability require their own evidence.

4. Reference Architecture and Operational Lifecycle

The reference architecture connects the properties in Section 3 to responsibilities, operational objects, and decisions about ongoing work. Its individual, collective, and lifecycle views describe the same configuration at different levels of detail. The organization is logical: responsibilities may be combined within an implementation or distributed across agents, services, and human participants.

4.1. Capabilities and Functional Organization

The seven capability families support perception, reasoning, planning, memory, predictive knowledge, action, and learning. Figure 2 connects their outputs: observations inform reasoning; plans and commitments guide action; outcome evidence informs further reasoning and experience analysis. Retained knowledge and, where used, world-model predictions support several functions.

These relations become operational through the acceptance decisions developed below. An observation carries its source and uncertainty into state assessment; a plan requires commitment acceptance; an action requires admissible dispatch; and a reusable change requires evaluation, acceptance, and context-specific activation. Capabilities can share supporting components while their outputs retain these different meanings.

Appendix B gives the supporting mechanisms, distinctions among information types, and the capability-to-property mapping. Property judgments follow Section 3.3 and Appendix A; the capability families organize supporting functions rather than additional assessment criteria.

4.2. Individual Agent Organization

Figure 3 separates an agent’s assigned role from the model, harness, and runtime supporting its operation. A role assignment identifies the responsible actor, expected contribution, decision scope, obligations, and period of applicability. Several assignments may belong to one actor or be transferred between actors. Actor boundaries follow Section 3.1.

The foundation model supports interpretation, reasoning, and proposal generation. The agent harness connects model invocation to context, memory, tools, validation, execution control, and tracing. The runtime supplies the execution environment for these functions. CoALA provides an antecedent for organizing model capabilities within memory, action, and decision mechanisms [2]. Here, the model–harness–runtime distinction allows several agents to share a model endpoint or infrastructure while retaining distinct assignments, contexts, permissions, and histories.

An agent operates on an authorized view of relevant state and knowledge. Its proposals enter the appropriate acceptance interface, which may be implemented by its harness, another authorized actor, a shared service, or a human decision-maker. Local context can remain bounded provided the evidence and conditions required for each decision are accessible. Updates affecting shared commitments follow the collective rules below.

Assignment history and configuration metadata link individual operation to the process record. Current state identifies who is responsible now; action and decision records preserve the actor and configuration applicable when each event occurred. Agent replacement, role reassignment, and component replacement are recorded separately. Their effects on ongoing work are assessed through the continuation conditions in Section 5.3.

4.3. Shared Responsibilities and Operational Objects

Five responsibility groups connect participating actors to the same work.

Agent Roles and Contribution Scopes assign responsibility for information, proposals, decisions, and actions, including which objects an actor may access or modify. An executor is the component or actor performing an execution step; its status as a separate actor depends on its responsibility assignment.

Plan and Commitment Management maintains dependencies, resource allocations, assignments, and accepted undertakings. Revisions account for commitments retained, changed, or released.

State, Knowledge, and Evidence Management maintains the accepted account of the work and the information supporting it, with provenance, temporal context, validity, and confirmation status.

Execution and Outcome Reconciliation connects authorized requests to execution and assessed effects, retaining discrepancies and unresolved outcomes for subsequent decisions.

Change Evaluation and Acceptance evaluates identified changes and records their acceptance and activation scope, including affected work and configuration dependencies.

The first group appears within the participating-agent view in Figure 3; the remaining four appear as shared responsibilities. These groups can span several actors or be combined within one actor’s scope. A concrete allocation identifies who produces, manages, validates, accepts, and uses the information in Table 3.

Table 3. Operational objects connecting responsibilities.
Object Information and operational use
Goals and Constraints Process reference, accepted goals, completion conditions, limits, and authorized amendments; predecessor or successor links where applicable. These records identify the undertaking and its accepted terms.
Roles, Policies, and Authority Actor identities, effective assignments, responsibilities, permissions, obligations, approval conditions, and authority sources. These records attribute responsibility and bound decisions and actions.
Operational State Progress, remaining work, resources, uncertainty, current assignments, execution components, configuration references, and activation or suspension status: the current accepted basis for organizing work.
Observations and Evidence Content, provenance, timestamps, affected objects, and confirmation status supporting state updates, monitoring, and outcome assessment.
World Knowledge Domain and environment knowledge with provenance and validity scope, used in interpretation and reasoning.
World-Model References and Predictions Model versions, inputs, assumptions, predicted consequences, and uncertainty, where predictions inform decisions.
Plans and Commitments Dependencies, assignments, allocations, accepted undertakings, versions, and execution conditions organizing collective work.
Action Records Request and work identities, responsible actor, plan, authority, execution configuration, dispatch status, assessed outcomes, unresolved effects, and request-correlated evidence.
Skills and Change Records Candidate, accepted, and active versions; supporting experience, evaluation and acceptance decisions, applicability, dependencies, activation scope, version-linked use and outcomes, and subsequent revision or withdrawal.

These are logical information structures that may be linked across stores or authoritative external sources. Agent, model, harness, and runtime versions belong to the relevant records or a referenced configuration. Process references and accepted terms remain connected to execution lineage under the identity rules in Section 3.1.

Record management and acceptance authority have separate assignments. Storing a proposal makes it available for assessment; the applicable role, policy, or delegation determines who may accept its operational status. Routine acceptance can be automated within a declared scope. A qualified state claim may remain uncertain, and a prediction retains its assumptions when used alongside observed evidence.

4.4. Interfaces and Responsibility Boundaries

An interface contract specifies how a contribution may acquire operational status. Building on explicit obligations and conditions at software boundaries [49], each contract identifies:

  1. the producer or requester, affected work and objects, and producing configuration;

  2. the claim established by acceptance, its qualifications, and permitted downstream use;

  3. the decision authority, delegated mechanism, and rule for combining any required approvals;

  4. the state, authority, versions, commitments, and environmental conditions governing assessment and use;

  5. the evidence and references linking the decision to its inputs, authority, dependencies, and disposition; and

  6. the handling of conflict, missing evidence, and uncertainty, including responsibility for follow-up.

Contracts may use executable checks, coordination protocols, or authorized human judgment. An applicable version can remain in use under an explicit compatibility rule; selecting the latest version is a separate deployment choice. Table 4 identifies the principal transition families.

Table 4. Interface transitions and their acceptance responsibilities.
Transition family Decision responsibility Conditions and resulting status
Observation →\rightarrow Accepted State Update Authority for the relevant state claim. Establish source, temporal scope, uncertainty, affected state, and valid dependencies. Retain qualifications needed by consumers.
Candidate Plan →\rightarrow Committed Plan Coordination and authorities for affected commitments. Combine approvals for the same proposal version and compatible dependencies. Establish joint feasibility, authority, assignments, and resource conditions; protect shared constraints when commitments take effect.
Action Request →\rightarrow Admissible Dispatch; Outcome Evidence →\rightarrow Outcome Assessment Execution responsibility and identified outcome-verification responsibility. Bind dispatch to current work, plan, authority, and execution conditions. Assess request-correlated evidence separately; retain partial or uncertain effects and follow-up responsibility.
Interaction Trace →\rightarrow Candidate Skill Experience-analysis responsibility. Identify the candidate version, source context, outcomes, assumptions, applicability, and limitations. The resulting candidate enters evaluation.
Proposed Change →\rightarrow Accepted Version; Activation Decision →\rightarrow Active Version Change authority and activation responsibility. Bind evaluation and acceptance to a version. At activation, establish applicability, compatibility, and affected-work conditions; record actual consumers and pending or partial activation.
Handoff Request →\rightarrow Accepted Responsibility and Admissible Resumption Handoff coordination, receiving actor, and continuation authority. Identify transferred and retained obligations, reconcile state and uncertain effects, establish compatibility, and resolve overlapping execution rights before dependent work resumes.

A family may contain several decisions and external operations. The rows identify changes in operational status; their composition follows Section 4.4.1.

4.4.1. Composition Across Acceptance Boundaries

A receiving activity uses an upstream result according to the claim established there, its scope, and its qualifications. It identifies the proposition needed for its own transition and the conditions that remain to be established. An uncertain observation can support investigation, for example, while a resource commitment requires an allocation decision.

For a receiving boundary bb, the required conditions are summarized by the guard

Gb=𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁b∧𝖡𝖺𝗌𝗂𝗌b∧𝖠𝗎𝗍𝗁𝗈𝗋𝗂𝗍𝗒b∧𝖩𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗍b∧𝖴𝗌𝖾b.\begin{aligned} G_b ={}& \mathsf{Match}_b \land \mathsf{Basis}_b \land \mathsf{Authority}_b \\ &{}\land \mathsf{Joint}_b \land \mathsf{Use}_b . \end{aligned}(2)

Here, 𝖬𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁b\mathsf{Match}_b requires incoming claims to support the intended interpretation, including uncertainty and confirmation status. 𝖡𝖺𝗌𝗂𝗌b\mathsf{Basis}_b requires applicable dependency versions, assumptions, and validity conditions. 𝖠𝗎𝗍𝗁𝗈𝗋𝗂𝗍𝗒b\mathsf{Authority}_b requires authority for the receiving transition itself. 𝖩𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗍b\mathsf{Joint}_b requires combined contributions and affected commitments to satisfy shared constraints. 𝖴𝗌𝖾b\mathsf{Use}_b requires conditions exposed to change after assessment to remain valid, or to be enforced again, when the transition takes effect.

The decision basis retains work and object references, upstream decisions, relevant versions, authority, evidence, assumptions, and the point at which the new status becomes operative. Equation 2 specifies a contract guard. Its enforcement and any resulting system guarantees depend on the implementation and environmental assumptions.

Where several approvals are required, the governing policy specifies their combination, required authority holders, and treatment of rejection or unresolved conditions. Approvals must concern the same proposed undertaking or change with compatible dependencies. Combining approvals for different versions requires reassessment of their applicability to the accepted version. One actor may perform several decision functions within its assignments while preserving their distinct meanings.

Concurrent acceptance must also protect shared constraints. Two allocations can each pass a feasibility check against the same available resource and still conflict when both take effect. Validation must therefore connect to commitment at the affected resource or state boundary, for example through a conditional update, an enforced reservation, or serialized admission. Checking separate proposal versions covers their individual records; the shared constraint requires coordination over the affected resource and interval.

The same requirement applies between acceptance and later use. A fresh read establishes the observed state at that point; subsequent conflicts require preservation, reservation, or a check linked to effective admission. An external interface bounds the effect that local acceptance can establish. Monitoring supports prevention when connected to such admission control, and otherwise supports detection and response.

Each consumer of an accepted result establishes its own authority and remaining prerequisites. Shared use of a record remains bounded by any limited allocation or execution right it represents. An upstream change triggers reassessment of dependent uses whose premises are affected. Earlier decisions remain in the history, with explicit disposition of existing commitments and external effects.

For transitions spanning several updates or external operations, the contract records completed, pending, failed, and uncertain parts against declared completion conditions. Downstream work proceeds only within the scope supported by that combination. Partial activation can be accepted for identified consumers under compatible conditions; completion for a wider scope requires evidence covering that scope. Later failure leaves earlier effects and obligations to be reconciled, revised, or addressed by authorized compensation.

4.4.2. Dispositions and Reassessment

The assessment returns accept, reject, wait for evidence, or escalate. Acceptance permits the specified transition; rejection records why the submitted transition is inadmissible. Waiting identifies missing evidence and a responsible owner. Escalation refers the issue to an appropriate decision-maker while preserving its pending acceptance status.

Deferred, escalated, or cyclic dependencies require a reassessment trigger and any applicable deadline or termination rule. Reassessment checks current state, authority, and versions. A timeout triggers this handling rather than satisfying an unmet condition. Independently admissible work may continue while affected transitions remain pending. Uncertain execution outcomes require the reconciliation described in Section 5.3.

4.5. Execution, Coordination, and Adaptation Loops

The lifecycle follows three interacting loops (Figure 4). Autonomic computing provides precedents for component interactions and feedback management [17, 18]. Here, the loops are connected through the operational objects and acceptance contracts of the ongoing work.

The execution loop selects the next admissible step, establishes dispatch conditions, and assesses resulting evidence. Local choices remain within accepted commitments and delegated authority. Changed shared obligations or invalidated assumptions trigger coordination.

The coordination loop develops proposals, resolves dependencies and resource conflicts, and accepts or revises commitments. Replanning can repair current work while leaving reusable behavior unchanged.

The adaptation loop analyzes contextualized experience, evaluates candidate knowledge, skills, workflows, or configuration changes, and records acceptance, activation, reuse, and subsequent feedback. Evidence for improvement comes from evaluation of the resulting behavior.

The loops may interleave, operate at different time scales, or remain inactive until relevant conditions arise. Execution evidence can trigger replanning or experience analysis; accepted changes can affect planning or execution after applicability and activation checks. A plan revision can invalidate pending dispatch, a policy change can affect activation, and an unresolved action can constrain both replanning and handoff. Receiving activities apply Equation 2 to these dependencies.

Changes in participating agents are handled through the same loops and continuation contracts. Computational Continuity spans their affected responsibilities. The property-to-architecture crosswalk appears in Appendix B.3.

4.6. Deployment and Resource Conditions

A deployment assigns the logical responsibilities to agents, harnesses, runtimes, shared services, external systems, and human decision-makers. For each transition, it identifies the mechanism provider, authoritative information source, acceptance authority, and owner of unresolved conditions.

Consistency and availability requirements follow the decision being supported. Historical analysis may tolerate delayed records; commitment acceptance must protect affected resource constraints, and recovery requires evidence about external effects. Resource budgets cover execution, retrieval, verification, and evidence retention. When a required condition cannot be established within those budgets, the affected work is deferred or its scope is revised under applicable authority.

Appendix B.2 develops placement choices, Agentic OS support, disconnected operation, and decision-specific consistency requirements. These choices preserve the contracts above while varying how their mechanisms are deployed.

5. Governance, Assurance, and Computational Continuity

The contracts in Section 4 locate decisions about operational status. This section develops their authority, evidence, and continuation requirements, including changes affecting work already in progress.

5.1. Roles, Norms, Protocols, and Authority

Governance assigns decision rights, execution authority, and obligations. Electronic institutions connect roles to interaction conventions [14]; role-based access control associates permissions and constraints with role assignments [50]. A configuration specifies each assignment’s scope, validity, revocation conditions, and escalation path. Least privilege and separation of privilege inform its technical enforcement [51].

Proposal, agreement, authority, and authorized action retain distinct meanings. Agreement establishes authority where an existing rule grants that effect to the participants. Execution also requires technical permissions, current preconditions, and compatibility with commitments. The configuration connects an enforcement mechanism to its authority source and identifies who may amend that basis.

AgentSpec specifies runtime rules through triggers, predicates, and enforcement responses [52], while GuardAgent generates and executes guardrail code against proposed actions [53]. Policy-following evaluation in τ\tau-bench and tool-output attacks in AgentDojo examine related enforcement and reliability problems [26, 27]. Their use within this architecture requires an authorized policy basis and a defined enforcement scope.

5.2. Runtime Monitoring and Outcome Evidence

Assurance combines pre-action validation, runtime monitoring, outcome confirmation, process compliance checking, and post-event assessment. Runtime verification examines observed execution against specified properties [54]; process conformance analysis compares recorded behavior with required procedures [21]. Pre-action checks use the admission conditions in Section 4.4.1, including protection against relevant changes between assessment and use.

Action records distinguish proposal, authorization, dispatch, processing, and confirmed success, confirmed failure, or an uncertain outcome. Cancellation, authority expiry, and late evidence are recorded against the request while preserving unresolved effects. Confirmation can also establish a specified partial effect. Its meaning depends on the evidence required for that action: request receipt, application completion, and physical completion establish different conclusions. The end-to-end argument explains the need for application-level evidence beyond delivery acknowledgments [55].

Outcome assessment uses request-correlated API responses, authoritative records, sensor observations, human confirmation, or execution histories, with source, time, and configuration context. Provenance supports interpretation and diagnosis [56]; agent identifiers, monitoring, and activity logs support attribution and inspection [57]. Partial observations can leave the required conclusion unresolved. Predictions and agent self-assessments can guide further checks, while confirmation of external effects requires evidence traceable to those effects.

MAST identifies premature termination and incorrect or incomplete verification among multi-agent failure patterns [41]. Each assurance claim therefore states the requirement, mechanism, evidence, supported conclusion, and limitation. Repeated-trial reliability and evaluation cost qualify that claim [26, 28]. Appendix B.4 distinguishes these claims from intrinsic self-correction and formal verification results.

5.3. Continuity Across Agent, Model, Runtime, and Shared Infrastructure Changes

A continuation decision concerns identified work under its current accepted terms. Process identity and execution lineage follow Section 3.1; resumption requires evidence that the receiving configuration can assume the outstanding work under current conditions.

Rollback-recovery protocols address consistent recovery, logged events, and interaction with external outputs [10]. An agent checkpoint can still precede an effect whose completion record was lost. Likewise, a missing RPC reply leaves execution uncertain [58]. Recovery must reconcile that uncertainty before a retry or establish applicable idempotency or duplicate-detection guarantees. Evidence about external effects and control of future execution rights address separate obligations.

Within the declared scope, accepting handoff or recovery requires:

  1. identifiable process reference, accepted goals and completion conditions, authorized amendments, current state, active configurations, responsible actors, and authoritative records;

  2. separation of completed, in-progress, not-yet-started, and issued-but-uncertain actions, with reconciliation or applicable duplicate-handling guarantees for retries and evidence of prerequisites for dependent work;

  3. compatibility of the receiving configuration with required state, interfaces, resources, and operational conditions;

  4. confirmed or re-established continuation authority, with the previous executor’s ability to produce overlapping effects revoked, restricted, or otherwise resolved; and

  5. a record of transferred and retained responsibilities, residual uncertainty, and conditions for resumed work.

Recipient-checked sequencers in Chubby provide a precedent for execution-right control [19]. Such controls address which executor may act; outcome reconciliation establishes what earlier requests already produced. Both remain relevant when a handoff is initiated because the previous executor is unavailable.

An infrastructure restart follows the same conditions. Restored records are reconciled with authoritative external information, existing commitments, and any remaining ability of the previous executor to act. Expired authority, superseded commitments, and obsolete configuration state are updated or excluded from the resumption basis. If a required condition remains unresolved, affected work waits or follows an authorized escalation or recovery procedure. Continuity therefore permits reconciliation pauses and applies to the supported changes declared for the configuration.

5.4. Governed Adaptation and Versioned Change

The adaptation loop produces candidate changes with supporting experience and an intended applicability scope. Evaluation examines an identified version against declared acceptance conditions; acceptance records the version, evidence, scope, and adopting authority. Activation establishes where that version becomes operative, using current dependencies and authority under Equation 2.

Evaluation addresses the changed object and its consumers. Documentation of intended uses and exclusions [59], retention, transfer, and interference [22], and configuration dependencies [60] inform this assessment. The change record identifies the proposer, evaluation and acceptance decisions, target consumers, activation conditions, and any migration, rollback, or compensation procedure. Changes to the evaluated candidate or its relevant conditions require reassessment.

Requested activation and established activation are recorded separately. Partial adoption identifies actual consumers, pending consumers, and ongoing work remaining on a supported earlier version. Mixed versions require compatible coexistence conditions. Later retrieval makes a retained version available for consideration; application requires compatibility with the receiving work. Its version, use context, and resulting outcomes are recorded for subsequent evaluation, revision, withdrawal, or deprecation.

Changes to goals, constraints, or completion conditions follow the identity rule in Section 3.1. An amendment records revised terms, authority, effective point, and the disposition of affected obligations and completed or uncertain actions. A successor undertaking receives a distinct reference and explicit treatment of inherited or retained obligations. Earlier outcome records continue to describe what was established under the terms applicable at the time.

Policy changes require acceptance under authority valid before activation. The candidate policy acquires force through that decision, preserving an independent basis for its adoption. Affected permissions, obligations, and commitments are then reviewed under the accepted policy.

Withdrawal or rollback also accounts for effects already produced. Restoring an internal version requires authority and compatibility with the remaining work; external effects require reconciliation and, where appropriate, separately authorized compensation. Sagas provide a precedent for compensating partially completed activities [61]. Compensation has its own preconditions, outcome evidence, and execution record. Idempotency, reversibility, and compensability remain distinct action properties.

Table A6 in Appendix B.4 summarizes the affected-work checks by change type. Section 6 applies the contracts and continuation conditions to the constructed trace, counterexamples, and configuration profiles.

6. Architectural Analysis and Integrated Worked Example

We examine the framework through a constructed production-order trace, controlled changes to its decision conditions, and implementation-source profiles of selected configurations. The trace specifies witnesses that would justify each transition; the profiles assess relationships visible in pinned source paths. These evidence bases support different conclusions. The analysis concerns decision requirements and scoped architectural findings, with implementation reliability and comparative effectiveness left for separate evaluation.

6.1. Scenario and Assessment Scope

Production order O1O_1 requires preparation, processing, and quality control under an accepted deadline, budget, and quality conditions. Its initial plan P1P_1 uses machine M1M_1. Alternative M2M_2 requires checks of availability, scheduling, and operating conditions; technically capable M3M_3 lies outside the current authority scope. Plan revisions preserve O1O_1’s accepted terms in the principal branch.

Four distinct agent actors carry interdependent responsibilities: Production Planning develops plans and allocations; Inventory / Procurement establishes material conditions; Maintenance assesses machines and usage restrictions; and Execution performs authorized actions and supplies outcome evidence. A Human Supervisor handles decisions within its assigned authority, including designated escalations. Shared models or infrastructure leave these responsibility boundaries intact.

The environment combines APIs and a legacy GUI. In the handoff, E1E_1 and E2E_2 are outgoing and incoming execution instances serving the same Execution actor. The instance change retains that actor’s responsibility; O2O_2 is a separate undertaking. The scenario uses one organizational authority context, obtainable but potentially delayed or conflicting evidence, bounded predictive representations, and explicitly introduced disruption branches. Authority and record sources serve as the reference basis; their compromise is outside these branches.

Appendix C records the assumptions, checking conditions C1–C7, and complete transition ledgers. Witness references specify required claims, sources, versions, temporal scope, and qualifications. Their satisfaction is stipulated along the selected successful O1O_1 branch. T11–T12 instead retain unresolved evaluation and reuse requirements. The trace is a specification-level construction under the claim-basis distinction in Section 3.3.

6.2. Integrated Operational Trace

Figure 5 follows the work through commitment, execution, disruption, continuation, and candidate formation. Step identifiers describe dependencies; independent activities may overlap. Tables A7 and A8 in Appendix C retain each step’s witnesses, decision responsibility, resulting status, and obligations.

6.2.1. Commitment, Execution, and Resource Revision

T00–T03 establish the accepted order terms, qualified operational state, and a candidate plan. Resource observations and predictive estimates retain distinct statuses. At T04, WP1W_{P_1} binds commitment to the same proposal version, applicable authority, and resource conditions protected when allocation takes effect. T05 confirms preparation completion and the start of processing on M1M_1; processing completion and quality control remain outstanding.

When M1M_1 fails at T06, Execution reconciles progress and identifies outputs requiring revalidation. Production Planning, Inventory / Procurement, and Maintenance assess M2M_2 against materials, scheduling, downstream dependencies, quality, deadline, budget, and existing commitments. In the selected branch, WrevisionW_{\mathrm{revision}} supports P2P_2, with affected commitments retained, revised, or released. Figure 6 shows this decision. Unresolved resource conditions defer the affected commitment; use of M3M_3 additionally requires an applicable authority change.

6.2.2. Uncertain Dispatch and Admissible Resumption

At T07, E1E_1 issues GUI request a2a_2 to dispatch the remaining processing to M2M_2 under P2P_2. Handoff begins before its effect is confirmed. The retained record identifies the request, work, plan, execution configuration, and unresolved status.

T08a uses WdispatchW_{\mathrm{dispatch}} to correlate an enterprise record with a2a_2, O1O_1, the processing stage, and M2M_2. In the selected branch, this establishes dispatch, leaving processing completion to separate evidence. T08b establishes WhandoffW_{\mathrm{handoff}}: receiving-configuration compatibility, retained actor responsibility, permitted continuation scope, and effective control of E1E_1’s overlapping execution, including treatment of outstanding requests.

T08c combines these results against current P2P_2 dependencies. The work resumes with E2E_2 and a2a_2 remains unrepeated. Reconciliation and handoff preparation may overlap, while dependent effect-producing work requires their compatible completion. Authorized investigation can proceed within its own scope while either condition remains unresolved.

Retry requires particular care. Evidence of non-execution must also establish that the outstanding request can no longer produce the effect. A retry under uncertainty would require an applicable duplicate-suppression guarantee covering request identity, delayed delivery, and the receiving environment. The legacy-GUI branch provides no such guarantee. Revoking future execution rights also leaves already admitted requests subject to reconciliation.

At T09, separate evidence supports the remaining processing and quality-control outcomes. Closure additionally accounts for the deadline, budget, and commitment dispositions. The selected branch completes O1O_1 under its accepted terms; missing quality evidence would retain the corresponding obligation and prevent successful closure.

6.2.3. Candidate Formation and Conditional Reuse

At T10, the actors derive candidate response skill s1s_1 from the O1O_1 trace. Its identified version retains applicability, resource and authority conditions, required evidence, and the distinction between effect reconciliation and admissible resumption.

T11 requires evaluation of that version against declared criteria, including unavailable resources, unresolved effects, and insufficient authority. The example supplies no evaluation result, so s1s_1 remains a candidate. T12 specifies later use in O2O_2, conditional on T11 acceptance, receiving-context evidence WuseW_{\mathrm{use}}, and an applicable activation decision. Actual use would link the version to the decisions or actions it informs and their subsequent outcomes. Evaluation, reuse, and improvement therefore remain open empirical questions for this pathway.

6.3. Controlled Checks and Counterexamples

Table A9 changes one decision-relevant condition at a time. K1–K2 examine proposal binding and the validity of prior outputs; K3–K4 separate request-specific reconciliation from execution-right control; K5 checks closure evidence; K6–K7 examine evaluation-version binding and receiving-context applicability; K8 separates feasibility from authority. The stated dispositions concern the first affected transition. They are analytical expectations, with later consequences dependent on any remaining controls.

A resource-allocation counterexample makes the composition problem explicit. Suppose M2M_2 supports one operation during interval II, and ca,cb∈{0,1}c_a,c_b\in\{0,1\} indicate two operative commitments. The shared constraint is ca+cb≤1c_a+c_b\leq 1. Both actors read the same unallocated state and independently pass their local checks. If acceptance updates their separate proposal records without protecting the shared allocation, both can become operative, giving ca+cb=2c_a+c_b=2.

The missing relationship connects validation to effective allocation for that resource and interval. A conditional allocation or equivalent controlled admission must preserve the shared constraint; a conflicting proposal requires reassessment, deferral, or rejection. This instantiates 𝖩𝗈𝗂𝗇𝗍b\mathsf{Joint}_b and 𝖴𝗌𝖾b\mathsf{Use}_b in Equation 2, while unrelated work may proceed under its own conditions.

Appendix C.5 examines the remaining counterexamples: unauthorized agreement, predictions accepted as outcomes, duplicate dispatch, overlapping execution, incomplete continuation summaries, overgeneralized skills, and trace retention without an experience-use path. Each identifies a missing decision relationship and the conditions under which it matters. Together with C1–C7, these cases locate evidence requirements across P1–P6; they provide neither an implementation profile nor a proof over all possible interleavings.

We apply Codebook v1.0 to three application configurations and one infrastructure boundary case. The assessment uses implementation-source evidence (basis I) inspected on September 29, 2026. Appendix D retains the pins, configuration boundaries, source locators, and criterion-level rationales. The assessment is static, with no framework execution or new performance evaluation.

Table 5 reports each property label and its criterion vector. Judgments follow Section 3.3: N requires a configuration-specific negative witness, while unresolved requirements retain U. Evidence from other versions or optional extensions remains outside the selected scope.

A diagnostic finding connects evidence to an affected decision, a supported conclusion, and a targeted follow-up check. Table 6 reports six findings. DR1–DR2 concern constructed cases; DR3–DR6 use the source dossier.
