DR3 and DR4 identify source-path limitations within the selected configurations, rather than observed operational failures. DR5 and DR6 instead identify evidence or scope requiring clarification; U provides no basis for asserting an implementation defect. In particular, historical skill retention and active dependency binding require separate inspection, as the Voyager witness in Appendix D.3 shows.

The result is a traceable connection between architectural questions and decision-specific findings. Established approaches combined as discussed in Section 2.4 could support related analyses. Comparative diagnostic accuracy, assessor agreement, assessment cost, and relationships to operational performance require the validation described in Section 7.6.

7. Discussion and Research Agenda

The analysis in Section 6 connects architectural relationships to specific decisions and evidence requirements. This section considers their implications across domains and the studies needed to assess the framework’s diagnostic and operational value.

7.1. Scope, Limitations, and Classification Validity

Agentic AI 2.0 provides a reference organization of established concepts for ongoing foundation-model-based work. Its contribution lies in connecting operational responsibilities, contracts, and criterion-level evidence within one analysis. The predecessor comparison in Section 2.4 identifies established approaches that can realize these relationships. The six-property synthesis remains revisable, consistent with conceptual-framework methodology [67]. Its minimality, exhaustiveness, and incremental diagnostic value remain open questions.

Profiles describe interdependent responsibilities within a declared configuration and workload. Equivalent operational relationships should receive equivalent judgments across software packaging choices; changes in actor roles, process identity rules, authority, environmental assumptions, or the changes being assessed may justify reassessment. Shared mechanisms can support several properties, with evidence required for each relationship. The resulting labels describe evidential situations rather than an additive maturity scale. Equation 1 fixes aggregation once criterion judgments are assigned. Reliability therefore depends on evidence admissibility, criterion completeness, and the applicability of negative witnesses. Documentation quality and source accessibility may influence those judgments.

The acceptance guard in Section 4.4.1 specifies how local decisions connect. Its implementation requires coverage of the relevant dependencies, authoritative version and resource information, effective admission control, and the stated behavior of external interfaces. Global consistency and progress under concurrent change and failure require separate implementation-level assurance, including observation of effects, outstanding obligations, and reassessment across connected boundaries.

The current evidence comprises constructed analyses and static source inspection. The production trace stipulates witnesses for its successful branch, while candidate evaluation and later cross-work reuse remain conditional. The three application configurations and the AIOS infrastructure boundary case provide traceable source findings within selected scopes. Their small, purposive selection limits generalization; independent assessor agreement and operational performance remain unmeasured.

The framework’s targeted source selection and retrospective construction also leave literature saturation and independent reproducibility of the synthesis open. Alternative splits and merges should be compared with configuration evidence and relationship-level judgments held fixed, following the broader concern with classification usefulness in taxonomy development [68]. Relevant outcomes include explanatory usefulness, assessor agreement, stability, and identification of consequential gaps. Comparisons should account for decomposition granularity and separate changes in the system from changes in definitions, grouping, or evidence.

7.2. Domain Implications

The prospective profiles in Appendix E apply the framework to enterprise productivity, adaptive manufacturing, and distributed mobility. They specify design and evaluation requirements; property-level support judgments require evidence from an assessed implementation.

Enterprise work places particular weight on accepted decisions, pending approvals, and responsibility transfer across business applications and human roles. The practical question is whether a case can progress or change owner with its obligations and decision authority intact. Manufacturing couples these obligations to physical resources, precedence, and quality conditions. A software rollback leaves physical effects to be reconciled, and rescheduling must respect work already performed and commitments to other orders. Mobility adds observation age, reachability, spatial constraints, and locally bounded authority. A delayed assignment may arrive after its original decision basis has changed, making communication conditions part of its admissibility.

These differences determine what counts as adequate evidence and which costs matter. Enterprise evaluation emphasizes rework, unresolved approvals, and supervisory effort; manufacturing adds physical outcome verification and quality; mobility emphasizes state freshness and commitment preservation during reassignment or disconnection. Table A14 develops these requirements under the continuation and reuse rules established in Section 5.

7.3. Coordination and Resource Constraints

Task allocation, distributed constraint optimization, and multi-agent path finding provide established treatments of assignment and joint feasibility [69, 70, 71]. The unresolved design question for ongoing work is how to maintain the affected commitment and resource dependencies as participants, capacity, authority, and information change. In particular, which dependencies must be represented to identify the smallest coordination boundary within which a disruption can be resolved?

Local repair is attractive when most work remains valid, but a revised commitment can affect allocations beyond the immediate task. Central coordination can simplify consistency while concentrating communication, computation, and failure risk. Local decisions can be timely while relying on stale or incompatible views. The choice of centralized, distributed, or hybrid control therefore depends on dependency structure, communication constraints, action reversibility, and the cost of conflicting commitments. Richer representations may expose more conflicts while increasing synchronization and maintenance costs.

Evaluation should vary contention, partial information, reassignment, and disruption, recording joint feasibility, commitment violations, resource conflicts, reassignment latency, and coordination overhead. It should also examine recovery from stale allocations and, under sustained contention, deadlock, starvation, and the distribution of service. These measures can reveal coordination failures hidden by eventual task completion and identify when additional agents improve useful parallelism relative to their coordination cost.

7.4. Memory, Prediction, and Grounding Uncertainty

Memory architectures can retain observations and abstractions for later behavior [72]. Ongoing work adds a retention question: which information must survive retrieval, compression, and transfer for a later decision to remain justified? Relevant items include provenance, temporal validity, superseded versions, unresolved source disagreement, provisional decisions, and responsibility for outstanding obligations. Evaluation should measure decision-relevant preservation alongside retrieval usefulness and context cost.

Partially observable decision models formalize action under uncertain state [73]. In the present setting, stale observations, conflicting sources, uncertain inferences, forecasts, and unconfirmed action effects call for different responses. Semantic uncertainty estimates can help detect unsupported model answers [74]; their operational use still requires identifying the proposition and consequences at issue. High confidence may accompany outdated information, while a reversible exploratory action may be reasonable under uncertainty. A single confidence value would obscure these differences.

Grounding proposals in available skills and affordances addresses action feasibility [75]. Permission and evidence of the resulting effect require their own checks. The research problem is to preserve these distinctions at manageable cost as information passes through predictions, summaries, plans, and handoffs. When evidence contradicts a forecast or supersedes a record, the system must identify the decisions and commitments that depend on it.

Longitudinal tests should track freshness, provenance loss, operational use of superseded information, calibration, and the effect of prediction errors on commitments. They should also measure unsupported state updates, outcome-confirmation errors, retries under uncertain effects, and appropriate evidence seeking, replanning, or escalation. Retention and synchronization costs belong in the same evaluation.

7.5. Governance and Adaptation in Open Environments

Distributed norm management addresses changing obligations, permissions, and prohibitions in open multi-agent settings [76]. For ongoing work, a central question is how revised authority or policy affects commitments already accepted. Delegation can expire, be revoked, or transfer across actors, assets, and jurisdictions. Resolution rules must specify whether affected work retains its earlier basis, undergoes reassessment, or waits for an authorized decision. Conflicts between an existing obligation and a new prohibition also require propagation to dependent work.

Adaptation raises a related question about the evidence needed to introduce change. Continual learning exposes interference between new experience and existing capabilities [22]; changes to prompts, skills, planners, routing, or models can likewise alter approval and action behavior outside the motivating case. Building on Section 5.4, research should relate evaluation and activation requirements to impact, reversibility, and applicability. Migration during active work must balance compatibility with timely access to fixes, with explicit conditions for version coexistence, handoff, and recovery.

Runtime assurance provides monitoring and reversion mechanisms for adaptive components [77, 78]. Extending this approach to agentic work requires attention to organizational authority, commitments, and reuse conditions alongside physical or technical operating bounds. Human review should supply a specified decision right or information need, with its delay and workload measured.

Evaluation should examine authority-revocation latency, propagation of policy changes, unauthorized actions, and detection of normative conflicts before execution. Change studies should test regression, applicability errors, effects on unrelated workflows, and recovery or rollback in the presence of external effects. The responsible configuration, applicable authority, and version-linked outcomes should remain traceable through these changes.

7.6. Evaluation, Empirical Validation, and System Realization

A validation program should distinguish the consistency of the assessment procedure, its diagnostic utility, and the operational effects of implementing the proposed relationships. This follows the design-science distinction between constructing an artifact and establishing its utility in use [79].

Assessment reliability and diagnostic utility.

Independent coding studies can assess the reliability of the procedure [80]. Assessors should use the same codebook version, configuration boundaries, and evidence packets. Agreement should be examined at criterion level before aggregation, since matching property labels can conceal different E/N/U judgments. Disagreement analysis should examine actor boundaries, evidence applicability, criterion completeness, the distinction between a scoped negative witness and unresolved evidence, and the conditions for continuation and governed reuse. Sensitivity studies should then vary system boundaries and evidence availability.

Comparative diagnosis requires a documented assessment procedure based on the composition of established approaches in Section 2.4. Assessors should receive the same case information and objectives, matched familiarization and evidence access, and randomized assignment to assessment conditions. Independently developed cases should include supported transitions, violated relationships, and deliberately incomplete evidence.

Reference judgments should follow each case’s operational contract, source records, and controlled observations where available. Diagnostic correctness should concern what that evidence justifies, irrespective of either procedure’s terminology or agreement with the six-property labels. Outputs should identify the affected decision, supporting evidence, unresolved or violated relationship, and proposed follow-up check. Evaluation should separate correct findings, omissions, unsupported absence claims, appropriate evidence requests, and the relevance of follow-up checks. Assessment time and evidence-gathering effort should be recorded separately. Table 6 illustrates this output format; an independent comparison requires new cases and assessor observations.

Operational effects and architectural costs.

Controlled implementations should vary whether a relevant relationship is present, weakened, or removed, then introduce conditions under which it should matter. Examples include contested resources, executor replacement, uncertain effects, policy revision, and reuse under changed conditions. These experiments should relate observed behavior to the assessed relationship and record interactions with other mechanisms.

The checks in Table A9 can supply candidate scenarios. Executable tests require concrete record schemas, interface behavior, event schedules, and independently observable outcomes. Fault injection should include delayed confirmations, changed resource commitments, version mismatches, and overlapping execution capability. Observed admission, pending, rejection, reconciliation, and obligation statuses can then be compared with the analytical expectations. Execution results and implementation conformance remain to be established.

Existing benchmarks can contribute environments and evaluators. AgentBench covers interactive reasoning and decision making [81]; τ\tau-bench combines user interaction, policy constraints, tool use, state verification, and repeated-trial reliability [26]. OSWorld evaluates tasks through external applications [3], while WeaveBench examines hybrid GUI–CLI/code workflows and trajectory evidence, including fabricated visual evidence [4]. Architectural studies need episodes that also expose intermediate obligations, responsibility changes, stale or contradictory state, uncertain outcomes, component replacement, and later reuse.

Task success should be accompanied by process measures selected for the domain: commitment satisfaction, resource conflicts, reconciliation errors, incorrect retries, authority violations, handoff correctness, recovery time, adaptation regressions, and supervisory effort. Comparative implementations should also measure storage and synchronization overhead, reconciliation delay, review workload, and change-activation complexity. These costs determine whether improvements in process integrity are practical.

Longitudinal realization and reproducibility.

Controlled stress scenarios should progress toward naturalistic deployments [82], including repeated work episodes under changing participants, policies, services, and operating conditions. This permits assessment of later knowledge use, responsibility preservation, and the benefits or regressions of accepted changes.

Reference implementations can expose the operational objects and contracts through workflow engines, agent harnesses, distributed services, domain infrastructure, or Agentic Operating System services. Comparisons should examine whether the required relationships survive these implementation choices. Studies should report assessed boundaries, component versions, enabled mechanisms, environment assumptions, workloads, codebook version, and supporting evidence. Retained traces and evaluation artifacts should make configuration changes distinguishable from changes in evidence or assessment, especially when external models, tools, and policies evolve.

8. Conclusions

Agentic AI 2.0 organizes established architectural concepts around the maintenance of ongoing goal-directed work. Its six properties, reference architecture, acceptance contracts, and criterion-level codebook connect operational responsibilities to the evidence needed for commitments, actions, continuation, and reuse.

The constructed analysis identifies decision-specific consequences of these relationships: local feasibility can leave joint commitments unresolved; effect reconciliation and execution-right control address separate continuation conditions; and retained skill versions require governed activation and dependency binding for later use. Static configuration profiles distinguish established criteria from those contradicted by scoped negative witnesses or left unresolved by the inspected evidence. Candidate evaluation and cross-work reuse in the worked example remain conditional.

These results provide an inspectable basis for architectural analysis and design. The next step is independent evaluation of assessment reliability and diagnostic utility, followed by controlled and longitudinal studies of concrete implementations. Such studies should relate architectural choices to operational outcomes and their computational, communication, and supervisory costs.

Appendix A. Codebook v1.0 and Assessment Details

Tables A1 and A2 specify the 21 constituent criteria. Their identifiers link the required relationships to evidence establishing E and counterevidence establishing N. Unresolved cases receive U under Section 3.3; property labels follow Equation 1.

A.1. Assessment Records and Reassessment

Each record identifies the assessed configuration, workload and work-episode boundaries, versions and enabled components, actor assignments, supported changes, and relevant authority, trust, and environmental conditions. It records the criterion identifier, codebook version, claim basis, applicability conditions, source locator and version, supporting finding, counterevidence, unresolved questions, assigned code, and rationale. Locators identify the relevant passage, code path, trace, or evaluation artifact. Implementation reports retain their provenance separately from direct source inspection or execution by the assessor.

For source-based profiles, criterion vectors follow ascending criterion identifiers within each property. The record separates what the source establishes from its interpretation under the criterion and identifies the configuration-specific path or constraint supporting any negative witness. Appendix D provides the records for the configurations analyzed in Section 6.4.

Reassessment distinguishes changes in the system from changes in scope, evidence, or classification. Changes to a criterion set, its interpretation, or the aggregation rule require a new codebook version and explicit reassessment. Preserving criterion-level findings allows alternative groupings to be examined without attributing a changed classification to a changed implementation.

A.2. Constituent Criteria

Table A1. Codebook v1.0: Maintained Process State, Collective Coordination, and Shared Operational Knowledge
ID Required operational relationship Evidence establishing E Counterevidence establishing N
P1: Maintained Process State
P1.1 Work-associated state is retained and made available to subsequent execution episodes. A state-retention and retrieval path tied to the work, at the assessed claim basis. Included execution episodes discard required prior work state or cannot retrieve it.
P1.2 The work account identifies accepted goals and completion conditions, progress, dependencies, unfinished obligations, and decision-relevant uncertainty. Representations and uses of these relations for the declared undertaking and workload. A required relation is excluded, or an unresolved condition is represented as settled.
P1.3 Accepted state updates follow identifiable acceptance and version rules that distinguish received information from the current operational account. Update rules and attribution linking evidence, acceptance decisions, and applicable versions. Unaccepted or superseded information becomes operative without the required acceptance treatment.
P2: Collective Coordination
P2.1 Distinct agent actors make attributable, interdependent contributions to the same work. Actor–role assignments and consequential contributions under the boundary in Section 3.1. The complete assessed arrangement has only one agent actor, or only internal component specialization.
P2.2 Responsibilities, dependencies, and accepted commitments are allocated and attributable to the participating actors. Allocation and acceptance relations identifying the responsible actors and dependent work. A required obligation lacks an assignment, or a proposal becomes a commitment without acceptance.
P2.3 Included conflicts or changed conditions lead to authorized revision, deferral, or release of affected plans and commitments. A resolution path connecting the triggering condition to an accepted disposition of affected work. Incompatible commitments remain concurrently operative, or required revisions bypass their acceptance conditions.
P3: Shared Operational Knowledge
P3.1 Information is made usable across distinct operational actors in carrying out their assigned responsibilities. Identified contributing and consuming actors, information access, and its operational use. The complete arrangement confines retention and retrieval to one actor’s internal components.
P3.2 Consumers can distinguish relevant information status, provenance, temporal context, and applicable versions. Information records and consumption rules preserving these distinctions. Information loses a required distinction or version context while being relied on operationally.
P3.3 Use follows applicable access and validity conditions, including treatment of conflicting or superseded information. Access, validity, and conflict-handling relations connected to the consuming responsibility. Disallowed, conflicting, or superseded information is used contrary to the applicable conditions.

E requires the complete criterion to be established at the declared claim basis and scope. The evidence descriptions admit equivalent realizations. N requires a configuration-matched negative witness; absence of a named mechanism or documentation silence is insufficient. Otherwise the criterion receives U under Section 3.3.

Table A2. Codebook v1.0: Governed and Grounded Action, Computational Continuity, and Feedback-Driven Adaptation
ID Required operational relationship Evidence establishing E Counterevidence establishing N
P4: Governed and Grounded Action
P4.1 An action is attributable to a responsible actor and applicable authority with an identifiable source and scope. Authority assignments and decision rules connected to the assessed action. The action proceeds beyond its authority or relies on authority established only by its own proposal.
P4.2 Specified execution preconditions and constraints govern dispatch, rejection, or deferral. A decision path linking applicable conditions to whether the action proceeds. An included action bypasses a required precondition or proceeds despite a failed constraint.
P4.3 The action path reaches the declared environment and returns observations attributable to the requested operation. An execution interface and environment-linked observations for the assessed operation. A placeholder or disconnected path substitutes for the represented environmental operation.
P4.4 Outcome acceptance uses action-relevant evidence; failures and unresolved effects remain explicit in subsequent decisions. Confirmation criteria and dispositions for success, failure, and uncertainty. Success is accepted from dispatch alone, or dependent work treats an unresolved effect as confirmed.
P5: Computational Continuity
P5.1 At least one identified interruption or execution-component change has a resumption path for work-associated state. A named change or interruption and its state-resumption path, within the declared scope. The claimed case loses required state, or the configuration affirmatively excludes every such path.
P5.2 Continuation identifies the undertaking and its accepted terms, and accounts for unfinished obligations and uncertain prior effects. Process references, amendments, obligation dispositions, and action reconciliation or applicable effect guarantees. A required obligation is dropped, or an uncertain effect is repeated without adequate reconciliation.
P5.3 The receiving configuration is compatible with the state, interfaces, resources, and conditions needed for the remaining work. Compatibility checks or established constraints covering the declared transition. Continuation uses an incompatible state, interface, resource, or configuration dependency.
P5.4 Responsibility and authority to continue are retained or transferred explicitly, with overlapping execution rights resolved and the disposition recorded. Assignments, authority conditions, and applicable control or guarantees for prior executors. Work resumes without applicable authority or leaves conflicting execution rights unresolved.
P6: Feedback-Driven Adaptation
P6.1 Feedback informs identifiable candidate changes or retained experience intended for later work. A path from feedback to a retained candidate or reusable experience object. The complete arrangement excludes cross-work candidate production or experience retention.
P6.2 Candidate admission depends on evaluation against declared acceptance conditions, with rejection or revision possible. Evaluation inputs, an identifiable candidate, acceptance conditions, and the resulting disposition. Candidates are admitted independently of a required evaluation or despite its rejection.
P6.3 Activation identifies the accepted version and applicability, and governs its adoption for affected work and dependencies. Version-linked acceptance and activation decisions, including the affected-work scope and dependencies. An active replacement lacks the required connection to accepted versions, applicability, or affected dependencies.
P6.4 Reuse is connected to the retained version and application context, with outcome feedback informing subsequent retention or change decisions. Retrieval, use, and outcome records linked to the reused version and follow-up decisions. The complete reuse path excludes the required outcome linkage or subsequent feedback treatment.

The criteria specify operational relationships rather than mandatory technologies. Authority may be delegated; compatibility may follow from justified constraints; and effect handling may use appropriate reconciliation or execution guarantees. A dedicated approval service, world model, rollback mechanism, or named evaluation suite is not universally required. Evidence and counterevidence are interpreted at the declared claim basis under Section 3.3.

A.3. Grouping Choices

The six-property grouping separates distinguishable assessment responsibilities. P1 and P3 could be combined as information management; their separation distinguishes the accepted condition of an undertaking from information used across responsibilities. P4 could be split into authorization and outcome grounding; their grouping attaches both judgments to the same action. P5 could be treated as a cross-cutting condition; it is retained explicitly to examine how state, commitments, effects, compatibility, responsibility, and authority connect across a component change. P6 could be split into experience retention, evaluation, and change governance; their grouping follows the path to controlled reuse.

Alternative splits and merges change the criteria aggregated under a property while preserving their underlying evidence. For example, established authorization and unresolved outcome confirmation can yield PS for grouped P4 when its other criteria contain no N; a confirmed violation instead yields NS. Splitting authorization from grounding produces separate labels for these findings. Comparison of groupings therefore requires retention of criterion-level judgments and explicit aggregation rules.

A.4. Boundary Cases and Realization Choices

Actor boundaries.

A single agent actor with several prompts, planners, critics, or stores may maintain state and recover from interruption while retaining responsibility within one assignment. P2 requires interdependent contributions from distinct agent actors, and P3 requires information use across distinct operational actors. Several actors can share a model or runtime; the assessment follows their assignments and consequential relationships.

Fixed procedures and selective adaptation.

A configuration may revise its current plan while deliberately keeping reusable procedures fixed. Affirmative evidence that the complete arrangement excludes cross-work adaptation distinguishes this case from incomplete documentation. Where an adaptation pathway exists, evaluation may justify retaining the current version or rejecting a candidate. The defining requirements concern the pathway and its conditions, rather than mandatory adoption in every episode.

Human participation.

An approval step supports the authorization relation established by the human’s decision scope. Its contribution to other properties depends on the responsibility, information, execution, and outcome relationships it connects. Direct human decisions and delegated authority are assessed under the same requirement to identify their source and scope.

Supporting mechanisms.

Checkpointing supplies retained execution state; its contribution to P5 depends on the continuation conditions in Section 3.2.5. Retained traces supply material for adaptation; P6 concerns their connection to evaluated change and later use. APIs, graphical interfaces, visual reasoning, multimodal interaction, real-time processing, physical controllers, and predictive world models are workload-dependent realization choices. Agentic OS services or existing infrastructure can supply scheduling, memory, access control, and lifecycle support. Their contribution is assessed through the operational relationships specified by the criteria.

Appendix B. Supporting Mechanisms, Deployment, and Change Details

This appendix supplies implementation choices and crosswalks for the reference architecture. The mechanisms illustrate ways to realize its responsibilities; assessment uses the unchanged Codebook v1.0 in Appendix A.

B.1. Capability Mechanisms and Property Links

Table A3 identifies selected property relationships for the seven capability families in Figure 2.

Table A3. Selected capability-to-property relationships.
Capability family Related properties
Continuous Perception and Multimodal Interaction P1, P4
Interactive and Visual Reasoning P2, P4
Social Reasoning and Collective Planning P1, P2
Shared Memory and Knowledge Accumulation P1, P3, P5, P6
World Knowledge and World Models P2, P3, P4
Grounded and Governed Collective Action P4, P5
Lifelong Learning and Skill Evolution P6

Links indicate selected contributions, with sufficiency determined by the constituent criteria. Governance and Computational Continuity constrain operational use across capabilities.

B.1.1. Continuous Perception and Multimodal Interaction

Acquisition can be event-driven, periodic, or on demand. Inputs include documents, conversations, interfaces, sensors, and execution traces. Multimodal interpretation may require representation, alignment, or fusion [83]. Observations retain source, event time, reception or processing time, and relevant uncertainty. Event-time distinctions help assess late or out-of-order information [84]; provenance connects derived records to their sources and producers [85]. Freshness, source authority, and scope inform conflict handling. Acquisition and interpretation produce candidate updates whose acceptance follows Table 4. VisualWebArena and OSWorld illustrate the interaction between multimodal observations and interface actions [3, 86].

B.1.2. Interactive and Visual Reasoning

Interactive reasoning develops and revises alternatives using tools, participants, and external representations. ReAct interleaves reasoning and action [1]; LATS searches alternative reasoning–action trajectories using feedback and value estimates [23]. Visual reasoning uses spatial or visual representations during problem solving, distinct from interpreting visual input or displaying an already derived result. Distributed cognition provides a basis for this use of external artifacts [12]; Visual Sketchpad supplies drawing tools used in subsequent reasoning [87]. Operational outputs comprise alternatives, evidence, assumptions, qualified predictions, and unresolved questions. These support downstream assessment without requiring disclosure of a model’s complete internal chain of thought.

B.1.3. Social Reasoning and Collective Planning

Proposal, critique, negotiation, feasibility analysis, and plan repair connect contributions from roles with different information, resources, and authority. SharedPlans and STEAM address collaborative plans, team commitments, and responsibility revision [7, 8]; AutoGen illustrates conversation-based composition of agents, tools, and human participants [24]. Plans retain versions, assignments, dependencies, allocations, and unresolved conditions. Permissions and obligations constrain their acceptance [9]. Collective Coordination is assessed through consequential, interdependent contributions by distinct agent actors under Section 3.1.

B.1.4. Shared Memory and Knowledge Accumulation

Memory can retain operational state, episodic records, semantic knowledge, and procedures [2]. Generative Agents illustrate memory retrieval and reflection [72]; Agora represents shared artifacts with lineage and verification status [88]. Operational use preserves distinctions among observations, hypotheses, accepted claims, decisions, and outcomes, including links between source records and summaries. Read, write, publication, and acceptance authority can differ. Linked or federated stores may therefore expose role-specific views while retaining validity, provenance, and material conflicts. Handoff additionally requires the obligations, uncertain effects, and continuation checks specified in Section 5.3.

B.1.5. World Knowledge and World Models

World Knowledge represents relevant entities, relations, rules, and constraints. Ontologies and retrieval-augmented generation provide supporting mechanisms [89, 90]. World Models estimate consequences through transition, process, constraint, simulation, or learned dynamics models. Dreamer illustrates learning and decision-making with imagined futures [91]; its actor and critic are algorithmic components whose separation has a different meaning from operational actor assignments. Where predictions are used, records identify model version, inputs, assumptions, applicability, and uncertainty. These predictions inform planning and can be compared with later outcomes while retaining their evidential status.

B.1.6. Grounded and Governed Collective Action

Execution channels include APIs, graphical interfaces, and specialized controllers. Toolformer studies learned API use [92]; WeaveBench examines interleaved GUI and CLI/code execution [4]. Runtime shielding offers a mechanism for restricting actions against specified safety constraints [93]. The selected channel determines which preconditions it can enforce and what its responses establish. Dispatch and outcome records follow Section 5.2; uncertain effects remain inputs to retry, recovery, and handoff decisions.

B.1.7. Lifelong Learning and Skill Evolution

Current-work revision, experience accumulation, and cross-work reuse have different scopes. Reflexion uses retained verbal feedback across attempts [29]; Voyager accumulates executable skills [6]. Agent Workflow Memory induces reusable workflows, while ExpeL accumulates insights and experiences [30, 94]. A-Mem revises linked memory structures [31]. Search-R1 trains search-tool use through reinforcement learning [32], and the agentic reinforcement-learning survey synthesizes a broader range of training approaches [33]. These mechanisms supply candidates for reusable change. Their acceptance, activation, and later use follow Section 5.4, with reported results bounded by each source’s configuration and evaluation.

B.2. Deployment Choices and Decision-Specific Consistency

Coordination may be centralized, distributed, or replicated; information may reside in shared stores, federated repositories, or authoritative external systems. Model services can be shared across roles or specialized by task, with corresponding contention, routing, and compatibility requirements. APIs, GUI actions, and specialized controllers provide different execution and evidence interfaces. Cloud, edge, and hybrid placement determine resource and communication dependencies. Human participation requires specified decision scope, presented evidence, and recorded effects on the work.

Shared infrastructure can group scheduling, context, memory, storage, tool access, permissions, observability, and recovery services. AIOS illustrates kernel support for agent applications [43]; the AOS proposal groups lifecycle management, workflow coordination, routing, and assurance in a runtime and coordination plane [48]. A deployment assigns acceptance and reconciliation responsibilities alongside these services.

Consistency requirements attach to supported decisions. Invariant confluence analysis provides a precedent for relating coordination requirements to operations and application invariants [95]. Table A4 applies this decision-specific reasoning to the proposed architecture.

Table A4. Consistency and availability conditions by operational use.
Decision and relevant records Conditions to establish
Retrospective analysis: Action Records; Observations and Evidence Delayed synchronization may be acceptable with identifiable provenance, integrity, and missing coverage. Establish completeness where the analysis requires it.
Allocation: Plans and Commitments; resource state Coordinate affected updates or use an allocation scheme preserving shared limits and existing obligations when commitments take effect.
Authorization: Roles, Policies, and Authority Use authority valid for the decision’s scope and time. Cached authority follows explicit expiry and revocation semantics, including during disconnected operation.
Retry, completion, or resumption: Action Records, evidence, state, commitments, and authority Reconcile request-specific effects and establish evidence for required obligations. Resumption additionally establishes compatibility, responsibility, authority, and effective control of overlapping execution rights.
Reuse or activation: Skills and Change Records; configuration metadata Establish applicable evaluation, authorization, compatible dependencies, and identifiable activation scope. Mixed versions require supported coexistence.

Requirements apply jointly to the objects involved in a decision. A single object can support uses with different consistency and availability requirements.

Disconnected activity remains within previously established authority, resources, and valid dependencies. Reconnection requires reconciliation before such activity updates shared state or commitments. Decisions lacking a required basis follow the dispositions in Section 4.4.

Context compaction must preserve access to relevant commitments, authority, uncertainty, and versions. Diagnostic sampling can follow the declared scope, while evidence required for acceptance or outcome confirmation needs an appropriate retention guarantee. Supported replacement also preserves the interpretability of records, permissions, configuration references, and outstanding responsibilities.

B.4. Assurance Scope and Change-Specific Checks

Assurance claims retain the scope of their evidence. Reported limitations of intrinsic self-correction concern reasoning without external feedback in the examined settings [96]; their application to external outcomes requires separate environmental evidence. Model checking establishes specified temporal properties of a model [97]. An implementation claim additionally identifies that model’s assumptions and its relationship to the deployed system.

Recent agent-system work addresses complementary recovery conditions: checkpoint and resume conformance [34], security-relevant dependencies under rollback [35], transactional tool execution [36], workflow retries and orphaned jobs [37], and event-sourced handoff [38]. These contributions inform implementation choices. Their coverage of commitments, uncertain effects, and continuation authority is assessed for the declared configuration using Section 5.3.

Table A6. Change-specific checks for affected ongoing work.
Changed object Acceptance basis and affected-work disposition
Goal or completion condition Establish change authority and revised terms under the declared identity rule. Record the effective version, affected commitments and effects, and any successor reference or inherited obligations.
Plan or resource allocation Establish proposal version, joint feasibility, dependencies, and authority at commitment acceptance. Identify retained, revised, or released commitments.
Knowledge or world model Establish provenance, assumptions, validity, evaluation scope, and active version. Reassess dependent plans, predictions, and decisions.
Skill or workflow Establish version-bound evaluation and acceptance, applicability, compatible dependencies, and activation authority. Record actual consumers, supported earlier versions, and version-linked outcomes.
Agent, model, or execution component Establish process reference, accepted terms, compatible state and interfaces, uncertain-action treatment, and continuation authority. Record retained or transferred assignments and resolve overlapping execution rights.
Policy or authority Accept under currently valid authority with effective time, scope, and revocation conditions. Review affected permissions, obligations, commitments, and prior decisions; re-authorize where required.

These are requirements of the proposed architecture. A revision to current work constitutes feedback-driven adaptation only when the relevant experience, acceptance, and later-use relationships are established under P6.

Recovery assumptions depend on the action model. Zhai et al. [98] analyze specification revision where incompatible irreversible effects can prevent satisfaction of revised requirements. Mohammadi and Bindschaedler [99] propose fleet-level accounting and admission control for irreversible exposure. Chan et al. [47] discuss rollback infrastructure and practical limits on undoing effects. Their respective scopes motivate explicit treatment of reversibility and compensability at admission, alongside the outcome and reconciliation requirements in the main text.

Appendix C. Trace Specification and Controlled Checks

This appendix records the constructed trace underlying Section 6. The ledgers preserve decision dependencies and witness requirements; their successful O1O_1 states are stipulated. T11–T12 retain conditional evaluation and reuse.

C.1. Assumptions and Trace Records

The scenario adopts six assumptions:

  1. roles and authority belong to one organizational context;

  2. relevant environmental evidence is obtainable, without assuming action success;

  3. information may be delayed, incomplete, or conflicting;

  4. predictive representations cover only the scenario’s required relations and retain their assumptions;

  5. changes to materials, machines, and execution components are explicitly introduced analytical branches; and

  6. process, resource, organizational, and interface details are restricted to the architectural questions examined.

Designated authority assignments and record sources form the reference basis, subject to observational uncertainty. Compromise of those sources and other model or infrastructure changes require separate cases and evidence. Each branch retains the initial conditions except where explicitly changed.

A transition record contains its identifier, process reference, before-status, proposing or executing actor, decision authority, input objects and versions, witnesses, guard disposition, after-status, and remaining obligations. Objects may use separate versions and storage transactions. The WW-references specify claims, sources or responsible actors, work and object versions, temporal scope, and qualifications. They denote required evidence rather than collected execution artifacts.

The trace retains O1O_1 through P1→P2P_1\rightarrow P_2 and E1→E2E_1\rightarrow E_2, with unchanged accepted terms and the same Execution actor. O2O_2 has a distinct process identity. Each receiving transition applies Equation 2; an unresolved required condition keeps dependent work pending, while a demonstrated violation requires rejection or revision of its current basis. Existing effects and obligations retain their disposition requirements.

C.2. Checking Conditions

  1. Identity and dependency binding. Decisions identify the intended process, accepted terms, and applicable object versions. Changed dependencies are reassessed before dependent use.

  2. Claim and outcome separation. Proposals, predictions, accepted state, requests, confirmed effects, and completed stages retain distinct statuses. A witness supports its established claim.

  3. Authority at the receiving transition. The actor and decision authority have the required scope for the commitment, action, change, or continuation.

  4. Joint feasibility and conditions at use. Commitments satisfy shared constraints; changing conditions are protected or checked at the operational point covered by the contract.

  5. Continuation with reconciled effects. Resumption requires an adequate account of prior effects, compatible configuration, accepted responsibility, and resolved overlapping execution rights. Investigation may precede effect-producing resumption.

  6. Obligation accounting. Replanning, handoff, and closure preserve unfinished work, unresolved effects, and commitments until explicitly disposed of.

  7. Version-bound adaptation and reuse. Formation, evaluation, acceptance, activation, and use identify the relevant version. O2O_2 establishes its own applicability and authority basis and retains outcome links.

Identity and obligation records concern P1.1–P1.3; actor contributions and commitments concern P2.1–P2.3; qualified cross-actor information use concerns P3.1–P3.3. Action admission and outcome assessment concern P4.1–P4.4, and T07–T08c expose P5.1–P5.4. T10–T12 specify P6.1–P6.4 relationships, with evaluation and reuse evidence still unresolved. This mapping locates criterion evidence requirements within the construction.

C.4. Changed-Condition Checks

Each check changes one decision-relevant condition while retaining the other branch assumptions. The reader can trace the changed input to its step, proposed status, and required disposition. Admitting the transition despite the stated gap violates the indicated condition. A pending disposition preserves the requirement while leaving eventual completion unresolved.

In the M3M_3 branch, the Human Supervisor can approve the change only within its assigned scope; otherwise escalation continues to an appropriate authority. Approval identifies permitted work and conditions, with consistent authority, plan, and commitment references. Resource conditions changed during approval require reassessment before commitment and use. Denial leaves the proposal inadmissible; a pending decision leaves dependent work pending.

K2 At T06, reconciliation leaves an M1M_1 output’s validity unresolved. Retain that uncertainty and require revalidation before using the output to satisfy a dependent stage. C2, C6
K3 At T08a, the record concerns another O1O_1 request and cannot be correlated with a2a_2. Keep a2a_2 unresolved; confirmation and retry eligibility remain unestablished. C1, C2, C5

C.5. Supporting Counterexamples

The allocation counterexample remains in Section 6.3. The following cases preserve the other conditional arguments. A later control may contain a gap before an external effect occurs.

Agreement beyond authority. Inspection is mandatory, and the participating agents lack authority to waive it. They nevertheless accept a plan omitting inspection. If Execution follows that revision without checking the unchanged obligation, completion violates the accepted terms. The missing check binds commitment acceptance to authority over that obligation.

Prediction accepted as an outcome. A model predicts successful M2M_2 processing before execution. If Operational State records completed processing and dependent work uses that record, the transition lacks evidence of the particular event. State acceptance must distinguish predictive support from environmental outcome evidence.

Retry after an unreconciled effect. An external dispatch has occurred, but the checkpoint predates confirmation. A receiving executor treats the missing record as non-execution and retries through an interface that accepts a new dispatch without duplicate suppression. Under those assumptions, the retry creates a second effect. Reconciliation or applicable effect guarantees must precede another dispatch.

Overlapping execution after handoff. Both outgoing and incoming instances can act on the same obligation after record transfer. Accurate state alone leaves conflicting actions possible. The continuation decision must resolve their execution scopes and effective rights. This addresses who may act next, separately from establishing prior effects.

Incomplete continuation summary. A summary omits a pending inspection or unresolved dispatch, and the receiver relies on it without consulting source records. The omission can drop an obligation or trigger an unjustified retry. Continuation requires decision-relevant completeness through retained information or traceable authoritative references, while allowing a bounded immediate context.

An exceptional response reused as a general rule. A successful O1O_1 response becomes an instruction to switch to M2M_2, stripped of availability, suitability, and authority conditions. In O2O_2, M2M_2 is already allocated. Accepting the recommendation without current resource checks creates a conflict; a downstream allocation check could contain it. The skill must retain its version and applicability conditions, with reassessment at use.

Trace retention without an experience-use mechanism. The complete assessed arrangement offers retained traces as its only adaptation mechanism, but supplies no retrieval, candidate evaluation, applicability assessment, or connection from later use to outcomes. The records support retrospective inspection; the claimed cross-work experience-use relationship remains unsupported. This gap concerns the adaptation claim, independently of whether either order completes.

These prospective design profiles expand the domain implications in Section 7.2. Table A14 summarizes the information, evidence, and evaluation priorities for each setting. Actor status for the listed participants and components follows Section 3.1. The continuation and governed-change conditions in Sections 5.3 and 5.4 apply throughout.

E.1. Smart Productivity Workforce

An enterprise work episode may span procurement, customer service, compliance, or internal approval, with interdependent tasks passing between people and software agents. WorkArena and WorkArena++ provide enterprise tasks and compositional workflows [102, 103]. OSWorld includes work across computer applications [3], while WeaveBench examines workflows combining GUI interaction with CLI/code operations [4]. A deployment may similarly combine structured APIs with browser or desktop interaction in legacy systems.

Stable policies and reference records coexist with case-specific correspondence, intermediate analyses, approvals, and exceptions. Their provenance and versions determine which information supports an accepted decision. A handoff must retain unfinished obligations and unresolved actions alongside the current artifact state.

Organizational roles provide an access-control basis [50]. Operational delegation further determines who may approve a payment, waive a control, or close a case. Technical access to a record should therefore be accompanied by the applicable decision authority and escalation path. Evaluation must include responsibility transfer and human supervision cost, as well as the final business outcome.

E.2. Adaptive Manufacturing

Manufacturing couples computational decisions to physical production [104]. Machine failures, new jobs, and processing delays motivate dynamic rescheduling [105], while reconfigurable manufacturing treats responsiveness as a system-level concern [106]. Allocation must account for precedence, capability, capacity, setup, materials, work in progress, and commitments to other orders. Revising one operation can change downstream timing and resource feasibility.

Digital-twin distinctions draw attention to the data flows between physical and digital entities [107]. The production-management API, machine-control service, or legacy supervisory interface must therefore be related to the physical evidence it can provide. A digital dispatch record and an inspection result support different claims about production progress.

Material removal, assembly, and transfer can persist after software state is restored. Recovery requires reconciliation of physical work and uncertain issued actions before a dependent operation or retry proceeds. Machine-use authority, maintenance state, safety restrictions, and product-specific quality conditions constrain admissible recovery. Progression through inspection gates requires the applicable quality evidence. Later reuse must account for changes to machines, control software, materials, production policy, and tolerances, even when the task description is unchanged.

E.3. Distributed Mobility

Mobility processes span assignment, pickup or service commitments, routing, reassignment, and completion. Autonomous mobility-on-demand and dynamic vehicle-routing research address changing demand and network conditions [108, 109]; multi-robot allocation provides a related treatment of assignments across available actors [69]. Reassignment changes both the receiving actor’s work and the commitments attached to its previous allocation.

Vehicle-to-everything communication introduces delay, bandwidth limits, synchronization problems, and temporal asynchrony [110]. Observation timestamps, provenance, and reachability affect whether a remote state report still supports a decision when it is received. Implementations should specify how long remote information remains usable and when local operation must defer, degrade, or escalate.

Authority depends on role, controlled asset, region, and operating conditions. A fleet coordinator may allocate work while local safety constraints continue to govern its execution. A deployment may permit completion of an accepted route during disconnection while restricting new commitments outside the local delegation. Handoff to another vehicle, controller, coordinator, or human requires reconciliation of active commitments, uncertain command effects, and responsibility. Recovery and reuse tests should vary traffic, location, communication regime, jurisdiction, fleet composition, and service policy.
